The fact remains that under the law as it is proposed now persons in Canada will be brought before magistrates and tried and if convicted will be faced with the alternative of either paying a certain sum of money or going to jail.
I believe the comparison made with Great Britain might be all very well, but even if the question of what is being done in Great Britain had not been brought up at all, the validity of the argument presented here this afternoon would not be any less. When a man is tried and convicted of an offence he may be given the alternative of paying a definite sum of money or going to jail for a definite amount of time. If he goes to jail, he is going to jail not because he has committed the offence in the first place but because he was unable to pay the fine imposed by the court.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: The prisoner is not given any choice in the matter, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
In relation to the remarks just made by the hon. member for Regina City, I would point out that if he would examine the British legislation I am sure he would find that the court is given a discretion in those cases to decide whether the accused is able to pay, and should therefore pay forthwith, or whether he is not able to pay and, as the hon. member for Prince Albert said, should pay by instalments over a period of time. We have the same discretion in Canada. He can pay forthwith or he can pay at a time to be fixed by the summary conviction court. The only difference is that it is not spelled out that it can be paid by instalments. If the time is fixed far enough ahead, there is nothing in the world to prevent the accused from accumulating, at the same rate he would pay the instalments, the moneys that are necessary to meet that fine. Therefore I say that, while I respect the motives for the speeches that we have heard this afternoon, I do not think they take sufficiently into account that under our present Canadian law the courts can give time to pay the fine. Not only that, but after they have given the time, if the accused quite honestly has not paid up the full amount, then he gets full credit for everything he has paid on that amount.
I am not saying that this is perfect. If the administrative authority wanted to go to the trouble of collecting instalments and that sort of thing and had the officers to do it, I am not saying it might not be better to so provide; but the time to provide that will be when much greater advantage shall have been taken of the present provision than has been taken so far by the administrative authorities.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: I was going to ask the minister a constitutional question, and one which he is able to deal with. It does lie within the minister's authority to set up a system of probation. Would he give us the approximate date when that might be set up?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
I dislike disagreeing with the hon. member for Spadina, but I think he is confusing the system of probation with the system of parole. The system of probation is a system under which, when the accused

is before the magistrate, the magistrate, instead of sentencing him to any penalty whatever, releases him on probation. Now, at that point in the accused's appearance before the court he has not come within any of our federal fields of authority at all. He is the subject of the administration of justice, a purely provincial function. It is only when he has had a sentence imposed upon him and he becomes either an inmate of the federal penitentiary system, which of course is under our authority, or the object of the royal mercy in the matter of the remission of his sentence, that he comes under federal jurisdiction.
At the present time, we have in our penitentiaries something which my hon. friend from Toronto Spadina seems to think of as a probation system. But our federal system is not a probation system; it is a parole system. We have had it in effect for some considerable time. Under a ticket-of-leave we release prisoners from our penitentiaries on the recommendation of the parole board to the John Howard Society, the Salvation Army, and other similar organizations. But these are prisoners who have been sentenced to prison and have thus come under our federal constitutional authority. They are released by us under that same authority.
But so far as the probation system is concerned, as I am sure the hon. member for Prince Albert would agree, it is a system under which instead of having a conviction registered or a sentence imposed upon the accused the magistrate binds him over under the probation officers to behave himself from that time on. All of this happens as part of the provincial administration of justice. Such a provincial probation system in Canada is the analogous body to that which in England has been responsible, as the member for Prince Albert has rightly said, for the great reduction in the prison population of Great Britain, and the great reduction in cost to the taxpayer. That is the body that looks after the collection of these fines on instalments and so on. I suggest that in order to make effective a law that we pass here for the payment of fines by instalments, it will be necessary to provide for it some such type of administration set-up.

I was wondering if the minister would care to comment on the suggestion I should like to make with regard to subclause 3. The whole discussion might be obviated if subclause 3 were amended somewhat along the following lines:
A summary conviction court may direct that any fine, pecuniary penalty or sum of money adjudged to be paid shall be paid forthwith or if the accused

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
Then, Mr. Chairman,
mention was made by the minister that the system in effect in the United Kingdom could not be applied here because they had probation officers, and the like. The system of probation officers was not established in its present form until after the original statute passed in 1914. The British act reads as follows:
(1)	A warrant committing a person to prison in respect of non-payment of a sum adjudged to be paid by a conviction of a court of summary jurisdiction shall not be issued forthwith unless the court which passed the sentence is satisfied that he is possessed of sufficient means to enable him to pay the sum forthwith, or unless, upon being asked by the court whether he desires that time should be allowed for payment, he does not express any such desire, or fails to satisfy the court that he has a fixed abode within its jurisdiction, or unless the court for any other special reason expressly directs that no time shall be allowed.
(2)	Where any such person desires to be allowed time for payment the court in deciding what time shall be allowed shall consider any representation made by him, but the time allowed shall not be less than seven clear days.
That is the 1914 act. I had the 1935 act here, but I lent it to Hansard. I suggest that this clause be allowed to stand so that consideration might be given to the drafting of an amendment, as a first step toward a very necessary reform in our country. The long discussion regarding the distribution of authority between the dominion and the provinces was, to say the least, quite inappropriate, and inapplicable to the arguments I have advanced.
The discussion this afternoon has at least brought about a review of the situation. I suggest this is one of the most important clauses to come before us. The clauses dealing with murder and other serious offences will not have such general application. In other words, comparatively there will be very few of those serious offences. The large body of offences in this country is that body in respect of which a fine is regarded as sufficient penalty.
In so far as the criminal law is concerned, when a fine is sufficient, I was glad to hear
Criminal Code
the minister say that imprisonment should not be enforced. He referred to the subclause as it now stands:
A summary conviction court may direct that any fine, pecuniary penalty or sum of money adjudged to be paid shall be paid forthwith or at a time to be fixed by the summary conviction court.
That clause as it now stands is honoured more in the breach than in the observance, simply because it is general and is not given ad hoc application, and in its present general form it has no actual mandatory application. Under the law in England, and particularly the 1935 amendment, the mandatory principle is applied. The minister has said that if a person were fined $10 with an alternative of twenty days, and could pay only $5, he would have to serve only ten days. Well, I do not think there is anybody in our country who wants to serve a jail term on instalments, or that the minister's suggestion helps the situation at all.
I cannot understand why my observations engendered such heat on the part of the minister because, after all, the generation of heat does not always bring light. I was glad the hon. member to my left, by his references, gave some illumination to the minister. I have tried to discuss the matter objectively. What I have placed before the committee represents a general demand with which I am sure the minister is in agreement. For this reason I suggest that this very important clause, applying as it does each year to more than 10,000 people in our dominion, deserves to be stood aside for the time being, to the end that, through a community of counsel, we may be able to arrive at some arrangement that would be satisfactory to the minister.

speechtext: Before this clause stands I should like to say a few words about it. I listened this afternoon to the many good suggestions from the other side of the house. I have been practising law in the province of Quebec for twenty-five years and I have always found that the judges and magistrates had quite a lot of discretion in cases such as we were dealing with this afternoon. I have also found that in the exercise of their discretionary power the judges and magistrates have postponed their sentences to give the poor people a chance to pay their fines. Sometimes they have postponed them for one month, for two months or three months so that the poor people were able to pay their fines and had not to go to jail. Therefore I do not think that the suggestions made this afternoon would improve the administration of justice in this country, as I said before. I say that from the bottom of my heart because I have always been on the side of the poor people, the weak and the miserable. But when we are dealing with justice in a country like Canada I think we should respect the discretion of the judges and magistrates and retain the system we have been enjoying up to date and which after all has not destroyed the framework of our community.

This clause is not greatly different from what it used to be but I cannot help feeling that this clause and the similar section in the code have omitted to correct a situation which has arisen not infrequently. Perhaps I could illustrate my point by giving an example. On one occasion the children's aid society in the city in which I live received a telephone call around midnight from a man who told them they had better come to get his children as he was going to shoot his wife and then commit suicide. There were several young children who had to be looked after.
The police were informed quickly and when they arrived there they found that fortunately the man's wife had not arrived home so he had not had a chance to shoot her, nor had he shot himself. But he appeared to have every intention of doing this, for a loaded gun was standing by the door. Apparently the wife was out committing some indiscretion. They were unable to do very much about it as the man in question had not threatened his wife directly. He had simply told somebody else that he was going to shoot her and they could not do anything about it.
He was held for a few days and I suppose actually the magistrate had no authority to do that. However, he was afraid to let the man out for fear he would carry out his threat. There have been several similar situations that have occurred and with which I have been confronted. This question of putting up a surety of $100, $200 or $500 to keep the peace means nothing to a person who has every intention of carrying out a serious offence like that.
In Ontario the administration of justice is helped somewhat by the provisions of the Ontario mental hospitals act, under which a person may be held for observation for sixty days when there is suggestion of mental illness. It rather cools them off. But where there is no question of mental illness and a person threatens to commit a crime, the situation is quite different. Another example would be line fence disputes out in the country where sometimes people get quite acrimonious.
I should like to see this clause stand and possibly the minister might consider an amendment which would permit a magistrate or a justice, upon evidence being presented that a person was likely to commit an indictable offence, to hold such person in jail

for from seven to ten days, a sort of cooling-off period. It is quite difficult to administer the law as it stands, because a magistrate does not feel he can hold a man, while on the other hand he hates to let him go if he may possibly kill someone.

I would like to address a few remarks now to those hon. members who this afternoon were so concerned about the position of a needy accused in a summary conviction court. These fees we are discussing here relate to summary conviction proceedings where the matters being adjudicated upon are often pretty trivial and no large' amounts of money or very serious crimes are involved. These fees we are throwing around in our discussion are fees which will have to be paid by the accused if he is found guilty-the same man the payment of whose fine by instalments we were discussing for some time this afternoon. The fees which are set out in this list were not arrived at by accident or carelessly. They received lengthy and very careful discussion before the special House of Commons committee on the Criminal Code last year. This committee took into account the fact that in very many cases it would be quite poor people who will have to pay these fees on top of any fine which may be levied. It was fully realized that the allowance to a witness would not be as high as he himself could otherwise earn in his ordinary work, as my hon. friend from Fort William has pointed out. But in view of the fact that most of these summary conviction cases concerned humble and needy people, we thought it was not unreasonable to expect these citizens who come in as witnesses to make their attendance part of their contribution as citizens to the administration of justice at this level. Unless the provincial authorities are prepared to shoulder the great bulk of these costs rather than the parties to these summary conviction matters, it means that the parties to summary conviction trials, who for the most part are people in pretty humble circumstances, will have to pay a burden of court costs altogether out

Criminal Code

To discuss the matter of the interpreter, for example, if this interpreter appears in a rural district he certainly will not be a person who is imported from any great distance for I agree that the fee that is indicated is certainly not exorbitant. On the other hand, if the costs are to be kept down that is about the amount that the traffic will bear. If he is in a city this amount can be charged in a case and there may be quite a number of cases in the police court in which he will appear as an interpreter in one day.
It was only after the most careful consideration by the committee that these fees were arrived at and although they do represent disadvantages in some respects, we think that upon balance it is better to leave them as they are. speechtext:
Some of the remarks made by the minister may change slightly some of the things I had it in mind to say about this schedule. Like the hon. member who has just taken his seat, I am quite concerned about the fee of $4 a day for a witness. It would not even cover his out-of-pocket expenses if he had to be away from home, let alone reimburse him for his loss of pay. When I looked at the schedule I actually wondered whether or not it had been considered carefully by the committee. It struck me that the schedule was something that had been carried over from a different form of society than the one in which we live today, a rural type of society where to be absent for a day from one's normal activity on the farm., or whatever it might be, did not matter very much.

Bu+ I do know that there is a different attitude today, particularly in industrial centres. Wherever possible a man is going to try to avoid becoming a witness or being placed in the position where he will have to be a witness because he knows if he is called he is going to have to forfeit his normal income for that day. His pay cheque is going to be that much smaller at the end of the week. I know from my own observation that in a good many instances citizens will take pains to avoid having to be a witness. Whether that is because of a lack of appreciation of the responsibilities of citizenship, and is something to be frowned upon, I do not know, but at the same time we have to be concerned with the effective administration of the law. That leads me to refer to the first part of the schedule. I am not very familiar with all the phrasing and I hope the minister will correct me if I am on the wrong track, but I take it that the fees and allowances that may be charged by summary conviction courts under the first part of the schedule are the type of fees and allowances which accrue to the magistrate.
Here again it strikes me that the concept is a carryover from the days when the magistrate was the country squire and a man of independent means. I think that is not altogether true today. I think the discussion we had earlier today on summary conviction revealed how important it is that the offices of magistrates and justices throughout the country be filled by men of high calibre. Let me refer to items 9 and 10 in the schedule. Item 9 is "hearing and determining proceeding, $1." Item 10 is "where hearing lasts more than two hours, $2." I take it from that that the magistrate is being paid at the rate of 50 cents an hour for the time he spends on a preliminary hearing in determining whether or not the man should be committed for trial.
People have observed to me that there are cases where the magistrate has received the allowance of $1 and at the same time the accused is paying his lawyer $100 to defend him and get him off. Perhaps there are two lawyers each getting $100, and the magistrate who has to determine between the arguments of this high-paid talent is in the position where his take-home pay is $1.
In view of the importance of attracting men of experience and judgment to these positions,
I think there is a very strong case for establishing a more suitable scale of reward for these men for the time they spend on these matters. Perhaps I am on the wrong track. If I am, the minister will correct me, but I think he will recognize the importance of what I am trying to get at.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
Whether my hon. friend is on the wrong track depends upon the attitude that society takes towards the administration of justice in a local community. In England they have excellent justices of the peace, first-rate men in every way, who serve year in and year out for nothing at all and count it a great honour to do so. No person pretends that the fees allowed to magistrates of that type in any way compensate them in a manner which would appeal to a more mercenary man. But if the magistrate is appointed by a government that uses good discretion in its appointments, I have not the slightest doubt that in most communities it will be quite possible to find first-class men and women who will count it an honour to discharge with great competence the important function of the administration of justice in their community even if their fees are only nominal.
When it comes to magistrates who are professional, those, for example, who sit in the larger cities, and who, try indictable offences without a jury with the consent of the accused, they of course handle a large volume of that type of work, and in all the cases I know of are paid quite substantial salaries because that is their only source of livelihood. But so far as these summary conviction matters are concerned, the whole philosophy of their disposition is that the people who act as judges will be substantial citizens in the community who will count it an honour, as they do in England and as they do in many places in Canada, to have the privilege of administering justice amongst people who in many cases cannot afford to pay high court fees. So far as my hon. friend's suggestion that the parties in cases of that sort are paying $100 a day to opposing lawyers is concerned, I am sure he will not resent my saying that his remarks disclose an unfamiliarity with the practice of law at that level.
The problem that we have here is a very difficult one. Everybody knows that these witness' fees and magistrates' fees are not adequate compensation for the time lost or work done. If they are made adequate, then it simply means that the disputes of humble people cannot be determined at all except at a cost which would be completely exorbitant for them to pay. This afternoon we discussed for an hour and a half how much time we are going to give a man to pay a $10 fine, yet we could easily enough run up to $40 or $50 in costs in connection with the same matters if we adopt an attitude that anyone who has anything to do with it has to get paid for the full amount of the time spent at his union wages.
Criminal Code
There is no way of handling this matter, except by the method I have suggested or by the provincial governments, if they choose to do so, coming forward with a plan to pay fees to witnesses and magistrates that are two or three times as great as these we are discussing and make up the difference by a provincial subsidy. This would leave the parties in summary conviction matters with about one-third of the costs actually incurred that they would have to pay.

Mr. Chairman, I think the ministers who have spoken in the debate established the fact that parliament had been given a fair warning. However, when an hon. member who attends as regularly as the hon. member for Ottawa West, and who was then parliamentary assistant to the Acting Prime Minister, was not aware of what was happening, there is some excuse for other members of parliament being unaware that this very important change was taking place. I do not wish to accuse either the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration or the Minister of Public Works of bad faith, but I think they are displaying very bad judgment. I think their remarks indicate, too, that the government is not likely to change its mind.
I believe the indication given by the Prime Minister earlier in the session, that this matter should stand until members in all sections of the house had a chance to discuss it in committee and decide whether the arguments in favour of moving to Montreal overweighed the very serious objections to the

proposals, should be kept in mind. The hon. member tor Ottawa West made a very careful speech, at the beginning of which he said, as reported at page 2578 of Hansard:
May I preface my remarks with the statement that in a general way I approve of the work of the national film board. I think it is very good, and has been well conducted.
I go a good deal further in my enthusiasm about the work of the national film board. Then on the following page the hon. member said:
In the main it has been very good work.
And then on the next page he said:
My criticism centres on the one point. I do not think sufficient preliminary matters were decided to warrant any decision as to whether or not the film board should be moved.
That point should be carefully considered.
I am sure all hon. members have read the submission to the Prime Minister by the mayor and controllers of Ottawa. While normally I am not greatly impressed by the opinions of people who have tax revenue to consider, I think that the Ottawa city council, who have offered the taxpayers of Canada the equivalent of a quarter of a million dollars, have made a gesture which should not be ignored. When so many people in the country are complaining about the burden of taxation I believe this gesture should receive favourable consideration.
As I suggested earlier, I think the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and the Minister of Public Works have had some bad advice in the matter, and that this evening it would be appropriate for me to say a few words with respect to the departure of this particular institution from the city of Ottawa.
I feel somewhat as if I were present at a funeral. I had a great deal of hope for the child, not yet fifteen years old. During the child's life the country was at war, and I think all hon. members will agree that the national film board did an outstanding job in helping Canadians at home and abroad to understand better the tremendous contributions being made by our Canadians in the army, the air force and the navy, as well as those on the home front-the factories, the mines and the farms. Without that contribution the Canadian war effort would have been less effective.
I realize that during that time the government received criticism for using this department to build up the prestige of the government. However, those criticisms were not taken too seriously; and the general effect was that Canadians were able to understand better what we were able to do collectively.
Supply-National Film Board
Speaking in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I intimated that at a later date I would say something about what it means to the people I represent to have this branch of government. I would like to tell hon. members that my constituency extends nearly 600 miles north and south and 100 miles east and west. In it there are only seven communities large enough to support banks. And if a community is not large enough to warrant a bank, the prospects for having a theatre are not too bright. Had it not been for the films produced and distributed by the national film board there are many people in that area who would not have had the pleasure of knowing what modern films are like.
I am afraid this move is going to make it more difficult for the people on our frontiers to have access to films, both as to the quality and the quantity, that they had in the past.
I was interested in seeing what the Canadian Chamber of Commerce had to say about the national film board. I find the chamber endorses the minority report with respect to the national film board presented by the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences. The chamber of commerce-
-recommends that the government instruct the national film board to place a larger proportion of federal government film production with outside film producers, and appoint to the board of the national film board two or three members as moderators with the duty of examining objectively the operations of the board and all plans for expansion.
The chamber recommends that the national film board should not extend its operations into fields adequately served by private enterprise.
The film act should be amended so that it is no longer necessary for departments of the federal government to secure their films through the national film board.
I cannot prove it, but I venture to say succeeding events will show that the movement of the national film board from Ottawa to Montreal will result in a much larger volume of government business being channelled through private film companies, rather than through our own national film board.
This reference by the chamber of commerce prompted me to see just what had been said by the commission. The membership of this commission would command the respect of all Canadians, and consisted of His Excellency the Governor General, Mr. Arthur Surveyer of Montreal, Norman A. M. MacKenzie, president of the University of British Columbia, the Most Reverend Georges-Henri Levesque, dean of the faculty of social

Supply-National Film Board sciences, Laval University, and Dr. Hilda Neatby, professor of history at the University of Saskatchewan.
I find that four of these very outstanding Canadians were able to agree on a report on the film board, while the fifth, Mr. Surveyer, who was not known to me, brought in a minority report. Before looking at the minority report it might be well to read what was said about films in Canada:
About 120 organizations in briefs and evidence discussed the work of the national film board, some at considerable length. Most of them approved of its work, and asked that this work be extended. They went further. Many Canadians expressed pride in the work of the film board considering that, like our national radio service, it is a valuable and distinctive Canadian achievement. We have heard much of the film board's Canadianism.
And further on:
The board is also praised for its services to distant communities: its films reach ". . . in a dramatic way many who would not otherwise come into touch with the culture of the nation". There is a corresponding regret and even resentment at the reduction of the board's estimates. "The present policy of restricting (the) budget can only lead to a cultural impoverishment of the people of this country".
In their recommendations they say:
We therefore recommend:
That the national film board be granted funds adequate for the necessary expansion of its field staff and of its distribution activities, and that the present policy of stimulating and complementing voluntary effort be continued.
And further on:
That the national film board continue its present functions as defined in the Film Act and that it continue to produce such documentary films as will serve the public interest. That the national film board continue its policy of commissioning films from private producers when this is in the public interest; that it continue and increase its efforts to co-operate with private producers and to encourage private film production in Canada.
And then finally:
We have observed with anxious concern that the various premises in which the film board conducts its operations are cramped, scattered, inconvenient and hazardous. In the interests of economy and efficiency, and in justice to film board employees, this deplorable situation should be changed.
That safe and efficient premises be provided without delay for the operations of the national film board.
That brings me to the so-called minority report, the reservations and observations made by Mr. Arthur Surveyer. His section on radio broadcasting that I am going to mention bears a great similarity to the briefs which come to hon. members from time to time regarding the plight of the privately owned radio stations in the country. But there is a section here on the national film board, and in view of the very moderate opinions expressed by the other four distinguished members of the commission I think

it significant that the fifth member should find it necessary to present a minority report. He does not call it a minority report; he calls it reservations and observations, but the Canadian Chamber of Commerce describes it as a minority report. He sums up his suggestions in this way:
I recommend, therefore, that the national film board should be required to give, each year, to outside film producers or to outside photographers, work to the value of half its yearly sales or of half the value of its annual production of films or of photographs.
This is the line that we have heard, ever since the national film board was started, from those who have argued that the government had no business getting into the field of film production; that they should leave it to the private producers.
When the first act was passed in 1939 one of the well-known members of the Conservative party, as it was then, Mr. Earl Lawson, expressed his objection. He of course made his position quite clear. He said:
I have in my legal activities represented many phases of the motion picture industry.
I am quoting from "Food for Thought" of March, 1950:
Having thus presented his credentials, Mr. Lawson advised the government to have its films "produced by Associated Screen News (of Montreal), or the other film concern, the name of which I don't remember."

Mr. Chairman, during this debate we have heard many speeches, some in favour and some against moving the national film board to Ville St. Laurent on the island of Montreal. So far we have not heard any speaker in the opposition give any good reason why the national film board should not be moved to Ville St. Laurent. I think all have evaded the question. I have noticed with pleasure that all those who have spoken have been unanimous in commending the work of the national film board. So did the special committee formed in 1952 to study the work of the national film board.
As has been said during this debate, under the National Film Act of 1950 the purposes of

Supply-National Film Board the board are defined as the initiation, promotion and distribution of films in the national interest, and in particular films designed to interpret Canada to Canadians and to other nations. I notice that it is designated as the representative of the government and of government departments in their relations with persons engaged in the commercial motion picture field.
Since we all realize the necessity of the national film board for Canada and Canadians, the question is how and where the national film board can best achieve its purposes. From what I have heard during this debate I gather that we agree with the report of the special committee on the national film board that the headquarters work of the board be centralized in one building designed and constructed especially to meet the production, technical and distribution needs of the board. The only point where there seems to be disagreement is the location of the building.
As we have seen, the purposes of the film board are to initiate, produce and distribute films showing the image of Canada to Canadians and foreign countries. To achieve these purposes, not only do we need a suitable building, but also we need the film board to be located where it can accomplish more.
During the committee proceedings in May, 1952, the location was discussed and the committee members of all parties were aware then that Montreal was the intended location.
To my mind, the national film board has to be located in a large cultural city, not too far from the capital city, where transportation facilities are available either by plane, train, truck or car and, having in mind the bilingual status of Canada, in a place where cultural and creative talent is easily available in the two official languages of Canada.
Even if Ottawa, our capital city, is a beautiful place, unfortunately it does not have the size to suit an institution of the character of the film board.
As to the very progressive city of Toronto, it surely has much to offer. It is a large city where talent is available, it is a cultural centre, but it has not the strictly bilingual characteristics that Montreal has. Montreal is a centre of both French and English culture. At the same time it is near Ottawa. It is a large city which attracts talent, artists, musicians, technicians of both cultures, because there they find more opportunities than they could find elsewhere.
With its seven radio stations in operation and another one coming in a few weeks; with its two television stations, one French, one English; with the C.B.C. international services, Montreal attracts both English and

French-speaking artists, musicians, actors, script writers, technicians, translators, narrators and so forth.
Montreal also has almost 500 schools both English and French. It has two large universities, McGill University and l'Universite de Montreal, 20 liberal arts colleges and many high schools. It has the benefit of 25 large libraries, 35 university and college libraries and 39 others. It has seven large museums. Eight newspapers, French and English, are published daily as well as many hundreds of weekly newspapers and magazines. There are also approximately 200 clubs where entertainment is found and which attract comedians as well as artists. There are 83 theatres, at least 20 cine-clubs.
Besides that there are about 300 active cultural and artistic societies among which are the Montreal repertory theatre, the Montreal women's symphony orchestra, les concerts symphoniques de Montreal, the Montreal festivals, the Montreal summer theatre, les varietes lyriques, the Canadian concerts and artists, les amis de l'art, the opera guild, the composers, authors and publishers association of Canada, etc.
Also you will find in Montreal many motion picture producers and studios such as the Associated Screen News, the M.C.R. Historia Film Production, the Quebec Productions Corporation, the Crawley Films Limited, and so forth.
These are only examples of how the board's creative workers would be in contact with people interested in the same field in both English and French. It would stimulate and facilitate their work in the initiation and promotion of films of truly national interest.
Since Montreal is not only the air-line capital of Canada, but also an important seaport as well as an important railway centre in Canada, distribution of films would be well taken care of.
Montreal has all that is required to help the national film board achieve well its purposes and it has been the one and only reason why it has been suggested to move it there. There were no other reasons. Much less the one mentioned in October, 1953, by the mayor of Ottawa, Miss Charlotte Whitton, who happens to be a good friend of the Leader of the Opposition and of the Conservative party. As a matter of fact she stated, as reported in the Evening Citizen of October 22, 1953, that the moving of the national film board to Montreal was:
All too high a price for Canada, the capital, and these families to pay for assuring the election, as the member from Ville St. Laurent, of Mr. Guy Rouleau, president of the National Young Liberal Federation."

Well, if Miss Whitton has the right to defend the interests of the city of Ottawa, she should do it as some other members in this house did it, on fair grounds. If her sources of information are always as good, I am not surprised at some of her statements against each and all, and I do not think that the people can take them at their face value.
Like the people of Ville St. Laurent, as well as the constituency of Dollard, I was shocked to learn of such unfair and untrue remarks made by a person holding public office. Nothing is farther from the truth. The people from my riding do not sell their votes; they are good and honest people who, when the time comes, vote according to their conscience for the party and the man they consider best fitted to administer the affairs of the country, and they have shown by their vote that they do not have much trust in Miss Whitton's best friends, the Conservatives.
Furthermore, I do not think that the Prime Minister of Canada and the members of his cabinet can be accused of having tried to buy the votes of my constituents. Their integrity is high above reproach, and that is why, even if only one national film board building should be built, 171 Liberal candidates, including the Prime Minister and the cabinet ministers, were elected on August 10 last.
And speaking of Miss Charlotte Whitton, I find it strange that the official opposition to the construction of the national film board building in Montreal started after the mayor of Ottawa spoke about the matter. Much stranger is the fact that during this debate they used many of her arguments. For example, one Conservative member, after hearing Mayor Whitton hint at bribery, said, and I quote:
The only talent that seems to exist in abundance in the city of Montreal is a superabundance of Liberal members.
Later, it was amazing to hear another Conservative member echo a statement made the previous day by the mayor of Ottawa to the effect that the moving of the film board, and I quote:
. . . would be the largest forced migration of persons in this part of the world since the expulsion of the Acadians.
But to be fair to the hon. member I must add that he realized that his political friend, Mayor Whitton, went a little too far and he was careful to add, "I think that is putting it rather strongly".
For a while during the debate, Mr. Chairman, I wondered who was the real leader of the opposition, the Leader of the Opposition sitting in this house, or the "never-stop-talking" mayor of Ottawa. If the matter were not so serious it would be very funny.

However, these irresponsible declarations have misled some people in regard to the real question at stake, and troubled others such as the person who sent a letter to the editor of the Ottawa Citizen under the signature "A film board wife", stating that it must be awful to live in the slums of Ville St. Laurent, in a place where there was no culture, art and so forth.
The moving in itself must not trouble that person very much because she and her husband have moved many times. Besides, the majority of those now working for the national film board have moved to Ottawa from places as far away as British Columbia. Furthermore, is it not part of the job of a producer of films to travel from place to place?
All that discussion is nonsense. The only reason for the moving of the national film board from Ottawa to Montreal is that Montreal is the best location in which that national institution can work in the best interests of the Canadian people and of Canada.
As to Ville St. Laurent, it does not take a back seat to any other city. The town of St. Laurent is very progressive and is now enjoying the most prosperous year in its existence. The town is divided into three distinct sections, industrial, commercial and residential, each completely independent of the others. This is an important factor which contributes to the satisfaction of all. The health-giving air, the easy means of transportation, such as buses, street cars and trains, the different schools, primary and secondary, and the low taxes all help the town of St. Laurent to expand continuously.
The Canadian National Railways line goes through the town, as do also two highways known as the Laurentian, and the Ottawa and Toronto, all of which run very close to the Montreal business centre, which is about three miles from Dorval airport.
The town of St. Laurent is also an up-to-date centre for recreation, and the new air-conditioned theatre, the auditorium with its capacity of 1,000 seats, the artificial ice arena, and its many public parks, all add to the enjoyment of the people residing there.
St. Laurent has a population of 30,000. About 75 per cent of the people are Englishspeaking, and 90 per cent of the Frenchspeaking people are bilingual. St. Laurent has beautiful residential districts with beautiful homes, and thanks to a good administration and to the efforts of this government through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation there are no slums in St. Laurent. It has modern schools and churches of all

I am sure they will not only enjoy the surroundings but also the spirit of St. Laurent because of the fact that we do not have a mayor like Charlotte Whitton. Mr. Chairman, we have all followed with a great deal of interest the present and past debate on this important matter. I believe it would have been helpful if we had received from the minister his interpretation of the purpose, policy and production objectives of the national film board, as well as his views on the desirable features of the proposed location of the administrative offices of the film board.
I believe most of us are basically in agreement that the national film board should be maintained, encouraged and assisted financially to achieve greater and improved production. But it does seem strange that so much significance has been attached to the location of the film board, and with other hon. members I fail to realize what remarkable features can be attached to the proposed location. The location of the administration body of the national film board is relatively incidental, because most films made by the board are made on location in various parts of Canada, and when interior shooting is required that is usually done in rented studios.
Personally I am very interested in the activities of the national film board, as I am in its big brother, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I believe that this agency, supervised by the government, is perhaps the most important one for the reason that it carries with it an extraordinary means of influencing men's minds and, together with radio, constitutes perhaps the most effective medium of mass communications.
To substantiate that statement there appears a very interesting index on page 16 of the annual report of the national film board for 1951-52. That index contains the non-theatrical distribution figures for 1951-52 as regards domestic showings, and gives the total audience which saw the productions


of the national film board. It is pointed out that during 1951-52 there were 151,196 shows seen by a total audience of 11,610,232. A little further on in the same page we have the information that national film board productions are distributed abroad theatrically, non-theatrically, through television, and through the sale of prints.
On page 17 we have a further tabulation of the distribution of national film board films abroad which indicates that there were 123,485 showings with an audience of 11,111,976 persons. In other words, if the last figures are used and added to the domestic audience during the year 1951-52 over 22 million persons received the message of the national film board.
Technically speaking, I believe that the national film board was initiated for the purpose of manufacturing and distributing informative and educational pictures, but I believe that there were other noble purposes in the minds of those people who initiated the founding of the national film board. I believe that the national film board was designed not only to help to unify the two ethnic groups that have been repeatedly mentioned in the house but all the ethnic segments of our Canadian people into one family, with each segment proud of the others. I believe it was founded to help Canadians of all racial origins adjust themselves to our society with the ultimate aim of making each of them believe that we value their contribution and that they as individuals are important in our democratic way of life.
I think that the national film board was also originated to quicken the appreciation of the Canadian people of the fine things of life, of the arts, music, drama, literature, in order to bring those things in greater abundance to our people. Surely these things are desirable when we consider the rapid pace of our everyday life where we seem to find so much accent on material things and sadly neglect our own cultural development. Fundamentally, certainly, it must have been the intent and purpose of those who initiated the national film board to use it to awaken the Canadian people to the great possibilities that exist to create a truly dynamic and individualistic Canadian culture. I do not think there is another place on this earth that has the ingredients to do so that exist in Canada.
Where else is there the deposit of human materials which exist here, the various racial and ethnic groups with their rich heritage of music, songs and customs, their various characteristics and emotional features which are indispensable if we are to have creative work? Where else is there the natural

beauty, and the landscapes which are also essential if we are to have inspiration and background material for significant works? But more important than this, Canada is one land that has freedom which is an indispensable ingredient if we are to achieve a new insight in the field of aesthetics and of culture, a word which is often used rather glibly and without caution. I know of no great work that was ever created unless it was a product of a free mind.
We Social Crediters are very interested in these things I have mentioned and in the activities of the national film board. We are more than just a monetary reform movement. We attach a great deal of significance to the film board because the ultimate aim of our philosophy of life and government is to create those very conditions which are conducive to gracious living, when men and women shall have the leisure to enjoy and partake of cultural pursuits and other worth-while human accomplishments.

I certainly appreciate your adjudication, Mr. Chairman, but may I point out that it is very difficult to talk about such a matter without also involving its implications. It is hardly fair for me to talk of the Stradivarius, for example, unless I am also allowed to say something about its tonal qualities. Therefore the question arises whether the move that is contemplated will bring about the objectives which we all consider as very desirable and possible. But in considering these things, I think we should remember that it was never the intent or purpose of those who initiated the national film board that it should ever become a political plum or a football. If that is to happen, I think irreparable damage will be done.
I mention these things because I have received many letters and questions with respect to whether this move by the government is intended to erase the indifference which our government seems to show toward all things "cultural" in our land. Is it a move that will correct that situation? I think these things should be considered because we are not dealing merely with pennies but with $5J million of the taxpayers' money. I think we should remember this when we are considering this appropriation. We should also
Supply-National Film Board remember that as one travels from one end of the country to the other one finds a deplorable lack of auditoriums and recital halls. Those that do exist, with few exceptions, are of the stock pavilion variety where one is often obliged to listen to a beautiful piece of music, Beethoven, let us say, and is constantly reminded that just a few days before it was the scene of the exhibiting of a prize bull.
I think we should also remember when we are considering spending $20,000 per acre for a new site for the board that there are hundreds of amateur drama groups throughout the country-I say "amateur drama groups" because the professionals cannot afford to remain here-and symphony orchestras, which were mentioned a few moments ago, that perform significant works of art. Yet I do not know of one of them that is not financially embarrassed and few can afford to acquire new scores or materials.
At this time we should also remember that while we consider it manly to visit art exhibits and fashionable to listen to opera, this wealthy country cannot point with pride to one national theatre or opera. At this time, we should also remember the very sensible and valuable recommendations made by the royal commission on the development of the arts in this country. Its recommendations have not been heeded. In considering this terrific amount of money that we are contemplating spending on the construction of a film board, I think we should also remember that hundreds of our young people are in exodus from this land to other places in order to find fame and recognition and, more important, appreciation of their talents. These young people are leaving our country to enrich the culture of other places because we show so much indifference to them. Therefore I ask in good faith whether it might not be advisable for the government to use this money to implement the production of the national film board or for scholarships and those things which are very necessary if we are to have worth-while cultural activity.
It seems to me that from the very beginning there has been a smokescreen about this whole issue. It would appear from private conversation with the various members that the government is intent on moving the national film board. I was just wondering, sir, whether it would not be advisable for the government, if they have decided on moving the national film board, to move it to a place which would be, for all time, an appropriate centre. I am quite objective about this. I do not refer to my own constituency, as other members have done in the past.

Supply-National Film Board
I believe that the government would be doing a good stroke of business if they moved the national film board to a site which is associated with visual beauty, and is symbolic of Canada. I refer to Jasper national park or Banff national park. When the giants of the cinema industry decide to make a colourful picture or when Hollywood intends to make a top-notch picture, those are the places to which they go and not to some city. At this time I also believe we should consider the point of view of the various responsible bodies in our community, which are not interested in political motives but the best interests of the country.
In this respect I have in my hand a letter from the Edmonton chamber of commerce, which is affiliated with the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. I understand that this letter has been forwarded to the other members, in common with whom I have the honour of representing the city of Edmonton. I quote:
. . . the Edmonton chamber of commerce deplores the action of the federal government in extending the activities of the national film board in competition with private enterprise; and, further, that it is opposed to this large expenditure of public moneys, creating more jobs for civil servants which could be absorbed in private industry; and, further, that this opinion be conveyed to the Ottawa board of trade, the three Edmonton members of parliament and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.
I have received other communications which point out that, at a time when the people of Canada are requested to continue carrying the heavy burden of taxation, and at a time when the veterans, the disabled and the aged citizens of this land have little hope of having their allowances increased, this government move is neither prudent nor an example of frugality. The national film board, as the name implies, is a national body that was designed to serve the best interests of all the people of Canada. Since we have to believe the move is made from political considerations, I think every member in this house would be wise to vote against this particular expenditure.

I shall not detain the house for more than a moment or two, but there is one point I want to make in connection with the remarks of the hon. member for Dollard. We had a somewhat unusual and I thought unnecessary experience in listening to those remarks. It seemed to me he went out of his way to drag into his speech and to criticize the mayor of Ottawa, whose name we all know and whose activities we all know. I feel that as a friend of hers, and a graduate of the same university, I should make some comment upon that.
I doubt very much if the member would have ventured to make those comments if Miss Whitton had a seat in this house. In any


event, I know I would not, and I doubt if any other member in this house would have the courage either. I say, therefore, that I regret very much that it was done. It seemed to me in very doubtful taste and judgment. I should like to say that I feel we should all remember that in whatever the lady did or said, it was pursuant to her duties as mayor of this city. I think, as such, they might have been kept out of this committee.

speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to make a statement. I think we can convey all the information hon. members require in the course of answering their questions.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
The first thing I had intended doing, Mr. Chairman, was to ask the minister if he was prepared to make a statement concerning policy and administrative changes in the Department of Public Works since he assumed the position of Minister of Public Works. From time to time during the past several months we have learned from the newspapers of certain rather important changes in the field of policy and also in the field of administration. I was hoping that the minister would at this time confirm, and probably elaborate upon, those reports. Such a statement would have assisted, I am sure, in giving us a clear and probably concise picture of the proposed method of operation of his department during the years ahead. Now, there has been one very important change in policy, apparently. It is about that change in policy that I desire to make a few comments tonight.
However, I am going to have to ask a question first; and if the minister's answer to that question is satisfactory, then, so far as I am concerned, it may not be necessary

for me to say all I had intended to say. My question is this: Do the proposed changes in policy which have taken place within the minister's department involve the abandonment of certain projects which have already been approved by the parliament of Canada?
Possibly before asking the minister if he would care to answer that question, I might be permitted to elaborate. I recall that last year the estimates of the Department of Public Works contained provisions for certain projects. Perhaps I should be even more explicit and say that such proposals were contained in the supplementary estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1954. Today we find no mention of a number of those projects.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext: Politics.

subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE

I would like to keep politics out of it-and I am saying that in answer to an interjection. I realize that, according to a press report, one change of policy the minister has brought into being, or intends to introduce, is that of asking for a lump-sum appropriation to be used for the purpose of acquiring sites and preparing plans and blueprints for certain projects.
Upon examination of the estimates of his department I find what I believe may be a figure designed for that purpose. However, I cannot be sure of this; and I am not prepared to wait until we get to that point, because if I do I may be ruled out of order and have no opportunity whatsoever to go into further detail with respect to matters of vital concern to so many people in Canada.
My question is this: Does the change in policy in the Department of Public Works involve the complete abandonment of certain projects for which provision was made in the main estimates last year, or in the supplementary estimates? Does it involve the complete abandonment of those projects?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
subtopic: REVISION AND AMENDMENT OF EXISTING STATUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, obviously the hon. member refers to the policy, to which reference has been made, of carrying in the estimates for a particular fiscal year amounts to cover the volume of work that it is expected can be carried out with respect to various projects in that fiscal year.
I do not think there is any great departure in that respect from the policy followed in the past. But, in reviewing the estimates, I did find that there were a great many votes that had been carried from year to year as revotes, without sites being acquired, or planning going forward, or any work being done. I thought it would make for more orderly presentation of the estimates and allow for a better scheduling of work if we included in the estimates and asked
Supply-Public Works parliament to vote funds only for those projects the department thought it could implement during the coming year, and to the extent that the work could be carried out. In order to enable the department to acquire sites, particularly in the smaller communities, and to advance planning, we are now carrying an item of $500,000 for the oncoming fiscal year, in vote 401.

Mr. Chairman, I think I shall have to be more explicit in what I have to say. In an examination of the supplementary estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1954, I find in connection with the province of Alberta that five projects are listed. These projects were approved by parliament on May 9, to be exact. Then, upon examination of the estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1955, I find no reference whatsoever to those five projects.
I am concerned as a matter of principle and, secondly, I am vitally concerned in another sense, because one of those projects was for my own home town. At page 26 of the supplementary estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1954, we find this: Acquisition of sites and preparation of plans for public buildings at Claresholm, Coleman-
I understand those two are in the constituency of the hon. member for Macleod.
-Innisfail-
Which is in my own constituency, and happens to be my own home town.
-Lac la Biche-
Which is in the constituency 'of Athabaska, represented by a Liberal member.
-and Vermilion.
Which is located in the constituency of Battle River-Camrose.
I should like to stress this fact, and I am speaking specifically of my home town, that the town council and board of trade, realizing the situation prevailing in that town with respect to postal facilities-this is no reflection upon the staff, for we have an excellent staff there, and I want to pay tribute to them-in view of the lack of facilities in the nature of a building, believe it their duty on behalf of the people in that community to take appropriate steps in pressing for favourable consideration for a new public building in that town.
I had the privilege of working with the board of trade and the town council and of accompanying their delegation to Calgary to confer with the postal authorities in the district office. I believe it is safe for me to conclude that post office officials at Calgary felt that a new building for that community

Supply-Public Works was essential, if the patrons of that office were to enjoy the high type of service to which they are entitled.
Representations were made to the Post Office Department in Ottawa by officials of the Calgary office. Obviously the Post Office Department in Ottawa came to the conclusion that if adequate postal facilities are to be made available to our people, consideration would have to be given to suitable quarters in that town. In fact, I am informed by the Post Office Department here that the project was put in "A" category. I am also convinced-and this is just normal procedure as between departments-that the Post Office Department must have been able to convince the Department of Public Works that the building was necessary for that community.
